newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX naysayers swept up by bullish crude move.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX naysayers swept up by bullish crude move.

text.p: Oil traders were forced to cast aside whatever bearish sentiments they harbored Monday after a day of unexpectedly wild trade that saw NYMEX crude nearly rise to its post-Gulf War highs, traders said.

Crude futures for November delivery on the NYMEX settled Monday a surprising 96 cents higher at $25.62 a barrel after hitting a contract high of $25.68 earlier in the day -- just shy of the $25.70 post-Gulf War high set this past spring.
News of production problems over the weekend at a BP America refinery in Toledo, Ohio heated the market up late Monday morning forcing skeptics to reconsider their positions.

That was the straw that broke the camel's back," said Nauman Barakat, a trader with Prudential Securities in New York, referring to the BP story. "Be long or be wrong. This is very much a bullish market," Barakat said.
Heating oil led the upward NYMEX charge on Monday, with the contract for November delivery gaining 2.64 cents and settling at 74.07 cents a gallon.

Gasoline also made an impressive move Monday, with the contract for November delivery settling 2.18 cents higher at 67.70 cents a gallon -- just a touch shy of a new contract high of 67.80 cents set earlier during the session.

News that rival Kurdish factions were again slugging it out in northern Iraq also fueled bullishness early in the day, amid views the fighting could mean further delays in the implementation of the UN-Iraq oil-for-food plan.

But some traders, even dismissing the significance of BP's problems with its Toledo crude unit, said all the news in the market Monday was rather light and was simply being used as an excuse for a market set on heading higher.
"The stories that are out there are dicey to say the least," said Tom Bentz, analyst with ING Derivatives Clearing in New York. "It's just that this market is in a bull mode."
Much of the oil market's strength on both sides of the Atlantic continued to be linked to tight supplies of middle distillates like diesel or heating oil, traders said.
Also, views both gasoline imports refinery output are lower than in recent weeks was fueling gasoline's strength.

Traders said the writing on the wall was in London, where crude futures for November delivery on the International Petroleum Exchange Monday set a new post-Gulf War high at $24.80 a barrel or 88 cents higher than Friday's settlement.

Also, traders looked forward with excitement to the American Petroleum Institute's (API) weekly inventory report, due late Tuesday after the market closes, for a fresh view of just how tight heating oil stocks are.
"If we don't get a build in heating oil stocks of two to three million barrels, this market could go to 80 cents a gallon," ING's Bentz said.
Heating oil stocks on the East Coast, the largest heating oil market in the world, are now at 24.5 million barrels, or 40 percent below year-ago levels.
"The new highs in gasoline and crude oil are definitely bullish looking," said Jim Ritterbusch, a trader with Sweeney Oil Co in Chicago.
"We're in store for very wide a choppy trade, but you've got to trade it from the long side by buying the dips and going long (heat-to-crude) crack spreads," Ritterbusch said.
The NYMEX November heat-to-crude crack widened Monday to $5.49 a barrel from Friday's settlement of $5.34.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
